title: Episode 238: Benjamin Franklin: The Lightning Rod, Poor Richard, and the French Alliance
description:
The extraordinary life of Benjamin Franklin: the runaway Boston printer's apprentice who tamed lightning with a kite, authored Poor Richard's Almanack, signed the Declaration of Independence, and charmed the Court of Versailles to win American liberty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we begin our monumental journey through the Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans with the quintessential American genius, philosopher, diplomat, and founding father: Benjamin Franklin.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RUNAWAY APPRENTICE OF BOSTON AND PHILADELPHIA
In 1723, a penniless seventeen-year-old runaway walked down Market Street in Philadelphia, his pockets stuffed with dirty shirts, holding three puffy penny rolls of bread beneath his arms, his mouth full of bread as he gazed at the strange sights of his new home. Benjamin Franklin was the fifteenth child of a humble Boston candle-maker, apprenticed to his abusive older brother James at a printing shop. Blessed with boundless curiosity and an insatiable appetite for books, young Ben read voraciously by candlelight, secretly composing humorous satirical essays under the pseudonym 'Silence Dogood', slipping them under the printing shop door at night to the delight of Boston readers. Fleeing Boston to escape indentured servitude, Franklin arrived in Quaker Philadelphia with only a Dutch dollar and a copper shilling in his pocket. Through relentless industry, spartan frugality, and charismatic wit, Franklin established his own print shop on High Street, published the Pennsylvania Gazette, and founded the Junto—a mutual improvement club of young artisans and thinkers who met weekly to debate ethics, politics, and natural philosophy. Franklin believed that individual moral virtue and practical public utility were inseparable, organizing Philadelphia's first subscription lending library, volunteer fire department, municipal police force, and the American Philosophical Society.  In Boston, young Ben had become a vegetarian not out of religious dogma, but to save money on meat so that he could purchase books on logic, geometry, and navigation.  In Philadelphia, Franklin invented the Franklin stove—a metal-lined fireplace that produced twice the heat with one-quarter the firewood—which he also refused to patent to benefit his fellow citizens.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: POOR RICHARD'S ALMANACK: THE VOICE OF AMERICAN THRIFT
In 1732, Franklin published the first edition of Poor Richard's Almanack under the fictitious pen name of Richard Saunders, a henpecked, impoverished stargazer. The almanac became an immediate publishing sensation, selling ten thousand copies annually throughout the thirteen colonies—a staggering circulation in colonial America second only to the Holy Bible. Between weather forecasts, tidal tables, and astrological charts, Franklin sprinkled memorable, pithy proverbs that forged the industrious character of the American middle class: 'Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise'; 'A penny saved is two pence clear'; 'Lost time is never found again'; and 'God helps them that help themselves'. In 1758, Franklin gathered these aphorisms into a masterwork preface entitled The Way to Wealth, which was translated into French, German, and Italian, read across Europe as the quintessential philosophy of self-reliant American democracy. Franklin proved that humor and practical wisdom could elevate ordinary working people, demonstrating that in the fertile soil of the New World, a person's worth was measured not by aristocratic pedigree, but by useful labor, personal integrity, and inventive intelligence.  Poor Richard's aphorisms were printed on broadsides that hung inside thousands of colonial kitchens and taverns, shaping an American civic culture rooted in personal accountability and thrift.  Franklin's Poor Richard was so influential that King Louis XVI presented John Paul Jones with a French naval frigate christened Bonhomme Richard in honor of Franklin's beloved pen name.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: TAMING THE LIGHTNING: THE KITE AND THE KEY: 1752
By the age of forty-two, having accumulated a comfortable fortune from printing, Franklin retired from active business to devote his life to 'philosophical experiments and amusements'. Turning his attention to the mysterious, frightening phenomenon of electricity, which European scientists regarded as an occult fluid, Franklin revolutionized physical science. He coined foundational scientific terms still used today: positive, negative, charge, battery, conductor, and armature. In June 1752, on a pasture outside Philadelphia during a gathering thunderstorm, Franklin performed one of the most famous experiments in scientific history: flying a silk kite fitted with a sharp iron wire, holding the kite string by an insulating silk ribbon from inside a cow shed, with a brass house key dangling at the bottom. As storm clouds gathered, loose hemp fibers on the twine stood on end; Franklin brought his knuckle toward the key, drawing a bright electric spark that proved beyond all doubt that atmospheric lightning and terrestrial electricity were identical. He invented the lightning rod, refusing to patent the life-saving device so that buildings, barns, and ships across the world could be protected for free. Immanuel Kant hailed Franklin as 'the modern Prometheus who stole lightning from the heavens'.  Franklin's scientific correspondents included Joseph Priestley, Peter Collinson, and Antoine Lavoisier, who eagerly replicated his electrical discoveries in European laboratories.  Franklin's electrical kite experiment was verified across Europe, leading Harvard, Yale, and William and Mary to award the former runaway apprentice honorary Master of Arts degrees.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE COCKPIT CONFRONTATION IN LONDON: 1774
For nearly two decades, Franklin lived in London as the chief colonial agent for Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and Georgia, working tirelessly to preserve reconciliation within the British Empire. Wearing tailored English wool and dining with members of the Royal Society, Franklin believed in the enlightened promise of the British constitution. But the relationship deteriorated following the Stamp Act and the Boston Tea Party. In January 1774, Franklin was summoned before the Privy Council in a dark, octagonal amphitheater in Whitehall known as the Cockpit. For an hour, before an audience of laughing British peers and cabinet ministers, Solicitor General Alexander Wedderburn subjected the sixty-eight-year-old philosopher to a venomous, humiliating public tirade, accusing him of treason and brandishing stolen letters from Massachusetts Governor Hutchinson. Franklin stood in complete, dignified silence, his hands behind his back, wearing a suit of Manchester velvet, not flinching or uttering a single word. When he finally walked out into the London winter rain, Franklin had ceased to be a loyal British subject: he had become a radical American revolutionary. He vowed that he would not wear that Manchester velvet suit again until he signed the treaty that acknowledged American independence.  The Cockpit hearing was intended by the British ministry to ruin Franklin permanently, but instead it transformed the sixty-eight-year-old philosopher into the undisputed diplomatic champion of American freedom.  During his London years, Franklin crossed the Atlantic eight times, measuring ocean temperatures with a thermometer to become the first scientist to chart and map the warm waters of the Gulf Stream.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE: 'WE MUST HANG TOGETHER'
Returning to Philadelphia in May 1775, Franklin found his country locked in armed conflict following the battles of Lexington and Concord. Elected to the Second Continental Congress, Franklin served on the Committee of Five alongside Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston to draft the Declaration of Independence. When Jefferson submitted his initial draft declaring 'We hold these truths to be sacred and undeniable', Franklin took his quill and gently amended the phrase to the immortal, self-evident formulation: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident'—grounding American democracy not in religious dogma, but in rational, universal truth. On August 2, 1776, as the delegates gathered in the Pennsylvania State House to sign their names to the parchment, committing treason against the British Crown, John Hancock remarked on the necessity of unanimous resolve. Franklin replied with his immortal gallows wit: 'Yes, we must, indeed, all hang together, or most assuredly we shall all hang separately.' At seventy years old, Franklin was the oldest signer of the Declaration, putting his life, his fortune, and his sacred honor upon the altar of human liberty.  When Jefferson showed Franklin the draft of the Declaration of Independence, Franklin also edited several small grammatical passages to enhance the rhythmic, musical cadence of the revolutionary manifesto.  Franklin's diplomatic composure was legendary: when Lord Stormont claimed the American army was defeated, Franklin calmly replied, 'That is not the truth; it is a Stormont,' coining a popular French slang word for a lie.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE COURT OF VERSAILLES: THE FUR CAP AND THE FRENCH ALLIANCE
In December 1776, Congress dispatched Franklin to France on the most perilous diplomatic mission in American history: to secure a military alliance with the absolute monarchy of King Louis XVI, without which the Continental Army of George Washington was doomed to defeat. Arriving in Paris, Franklin performed a stroke of public relations genius: setting aside courtly wigs and lace, he presented himself in simple brown homespun coats and an oversized Canadian marten-fur cap, playing the role of the virtuous, uncorrupted philosopher-sage of the American wilderness. The French public went wild: Franklin's portrait appeared on porcelain snuffboxes, rings, medallions, and watches; crowds followed him through the streets of Paris shouting 'Vive Franklin!'. In the gilded salons of Versailles, Franklin charmed Marie Antoinette and foreign minister Vergennes. When news arrived of the American victory at Saratoga in late 1777, Franklin capitalized on the moment, negotiating the Treaty of Alliance of 1778, securing French naval fleets, siege artillery, and thousands of French soldiers under Rochambeau and Lafayette that made the final triumph at Yorktown possible.  French women adopted high coiffure hairstyles known as 'coiffures à la Franklin', shaped like lightning conductors to honor the American philosopher who had conquered the thunderbolts.  In Paris, Franklin lived in a comfortable mansion in the village of Passy, where he set up a private printing press in his garden, printing satirical diplomatic hoaxes to promote the American cause.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE CONSTITUTIONAL CONVENTION AND THE RISING SUN: 1787
In 1787, at the age of eighty-one, suffering from painful gout and kidney stones that required him to be carried through Philadelphia streets in a sedan chair borne by four prisoners, Franklin attended the Constitutional Convention. As the revered elder statesman, Franklin repeatedly mediated bitter disputes between large and small states, urging delegates to set aside personal pride and doubt their own infallibility for the sake of the union. On the final day, September 17, 1787, as the delegates stepped forward to sign the newly drafted United States Constitution, Franklin looked toward the president's chair behind George Washington, which had a decorative sunburst carved into the mahogany backrest. Franklin remarked to the colleagues around him: 'Painters have found it difficult to distinguish in their art a rising from a setting sun. I have often and often in the course of the session looked at that behind the President without being able to tell whether it was rising or setting: but now at length I have the happiness to know that it is a rising and not a setting sun.' When Franklin died in April 1790 at the age of eighty-four, twenty thousand mourners attended his funeral in Philadelphia, celebrating the poor candle-maker's boy who had snatched lightning from the sky and the scepter from tyrants.  In his final public act in February 1790, Franklin signed a passionate petition to the United States Congress on behalf of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society, urging the immediate abolition of slavery.  Franklin was the only founding father to sign all four foundational documents of the American Republic: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 239: Alexander Hamilton—The Immigrant Bastard, the Treasury, the Federalist Papers, and the Fatal Duel at Weehawken. Until then, stay curious.
